:::{#thm-taylor-mv}
#### Second-order Taylor theorem in several variables

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$ have first and second partial derivatives
that are continuous on $\reals^p$ ([continuity](vector-calculus.qmd#def-continuous-several)),
and let $\vecf{z}, \vecf{h} \in \reals^p$.
Then there is a $\tau \in (0, 1)$ with

$$
f(\vecf{z} + \vecf{h})
= f(\vecf{z})
+ \tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vecf{z})}} \vecf{h}
+ \frac{1}{2}\,\tp{\vecf{h}}\,\matr{H}_f(\vecf{z} + \tau \vecf{h})\,\vecf{h}.
$$

:::

::: proof

Let $g(t) \eqdef f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})$ for $t \in \reals$,
the values of $f$ along the line through $\vecf{z}$ in the direction $\vecf{h}$.
The [inner function](sets-functions.qmd#def-composition) $\vy(t) = \vecf{z} + t \vecf{h}$ has entries $y_j = z_j + t h_j$,
so $\deriv{t} y_j = h_j$, and its derivative ([vector-valued derivative](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-valued-derivative)) is the $1 \times p$ matrix $\tp{\vecf{h}}$.
By the vector chain rule ([vector chain rule](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-chain-vec), with its input $t$ of length $1$,
its inner function $\vy(t) = \vecf{z} + t \vecf{h}$, and its outer function $f$),

$$
\ba
g'(t)
&= \tp{\vecf{h}}\,\deriv{\vx} f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})
&& \text{(vector chain rule)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} h_j\,\deriv{x_j} f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h}).
&& \text{(matrix product)}
\ea
$$

The second step writes out the [matrix product](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-mult).
$g'$ is continuous ([continuity](vector-calculus.qmd#def-continuous-several)):
$t \mapsto \vecf{z} + t \vecf{h}$ is continuous, since $\norm{(\vecf{z} + s \vecf{h}) - (\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})} = \abs{s - t}\,\norm{\vecf{h}}$,
each $\deriv{x_j} f$ is continuous by assumption,
and compositions, sums and constant multiples of continuous functions are continuous.
Each $\deriv{x_j} f$ has continuous partial derivatives, the second partial derivatives of $f$,
so the same chain-rule computation applies to it:
$\deriv{t} \sb{\deriv{x_j} f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})} = \sum_{i=1}^{p} h_i\,\deriv{x_i} \paren{\deriv{x_j} f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})}$.
So

$$
\ba
g''(t)
&= \sum_{j=1}^{p} h_j \sum_{i=1}^{p} h_i\,\deriv{x_i} \paren{\deriv{x_j} f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})}
&& \text{(differentiate each term of } g'(t) \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sum_{j=1}^{p} h_i\,\sb{\matr{H}_f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})}_{ij}\,h_j
&& \text{(definition of the Hessian; reorder the finite sums)}
\\
&= \tp{\vecf{h}}\,\matr{H}_f(\vecf{z} + t \vecf{h})\,\vecf{h}.
&& \text{(matrix product)}
\ea
$$

The last step is again the [matrix product](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-mult).
Now apply @thm-taylor-1d to $g$ on $[0, 1]$:
there is a $\tau \in (0, 1)$ with

$$
\ba
f(\vecf{z} + \vecf{h})
&= g(1)
&& \text{(definition of } g \text{)}
\\
&= g(0) + g'(0)\,(1 - 0) + \frac{1}{2}\,g''(\tau)\,(1 - 0)^2
&& \text{(@thm-taylor-1d, with } a = 0, b = 1 \text{)}
\\
&= g(0) + g'(0) + \frac{1}{2}\,g''(\tau)
&& \text{(} 1 - 0 = 1 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\vecf{h}}\,\deriv{\vx} f(\vecf{z}) + \frac{1}{2}\,\tp{\vecf{h}}\,\matr{H}_f(\vecf{z} + \tau \vecf{h})\,\vecf{h}
&& \text{(substitute } g(0), g'(0), g''(\tau) \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vecf{z}) + \tp{\paren{\deriv{\vx} f(\vecf{z})}} \vecf{h} + \frac{1}{2}\,\tp{\vecf{h}}\,\matr{H}_f(\vecf{z} + \tau \vecf{h})\,\vecf{h}.
&& \text{(a } 1 \times 1 \text{ matrix equals its transpose)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-taylor-mv}
#### For a quadratic form the expansion is exact

Let $f(\vx) = \tp{\vx} \matr{S} \vx$ with $\matr{S}$ symmetric and constant.
Its gradient is $2 \matr{S} \vx$ ([derivative of a quadratic form](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-quadratic-form))
and its Hessian is $2 \matr{S}$ at every point ([Hessian of a quadratic form](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-hessian-quadratic)),
so whatever $\tau$ is, @thm-taylor-mv reads

$$
f(\vecf{z} + \vecf{h}) = \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} + \tp{(2 \matr{S} \vecf{z})} \vecf{h} + \frac{1}{2}\,\tp{\vecf{h}} (2 \matr{S}) \vecf{h}
= \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} + 2\,\tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{h} + \tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{h},
$$

using $\tp{(2 \matr{S} \vecf{z})} = 2\,\tp{\vecf{z}}\,\tp{\matr{S}} = 2\,\tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S}$.
Multiplying out directly gives the same:

$$
\ba
\tp{(\vecf{z} + \vecf{h})} \matr{S} (\vecf{z} + \vecf{h})
&= \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} + \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{h} + \tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} + \tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{h}
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} + 2\,\tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{h} + \tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{h}.
&& \text{(} \tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{z} = \tp{(\tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{S} \vecf{z})} = \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{S} \vecf{h} \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::
